title: Pauri 7, meaning: fame without grace
hook: live four ages and be famous everywhere; without His kindly glance, no one asks after you (Japji 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri seven. Your line was je jug chaare: if your life lasted all four ages, and ten times more. Today, the turn. Day one hundred seventy-six.

Everyone has checked the numbers at least once. How many people liked the photo. How many people read your post. Whether anyone noticed the thing you worked so hard on. It's human to want to be seen, and a little embarrassing how much it can sting when you aren't. Now imagine the biggest version of that possible: famous everywhere on earth, for thousands of years. Guru Nanak's seventh pauri imagines exactly that, and then asks one quiet question about it.
screen: `CHECKING THE NUMBERS.` → `FAMOUS EVERYWHERE, FOREVER.` → `ONE QUIET QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. If your life lasted the four ages, and ten times more; if you were known in all nine regions of the world, and everyone walked along with you; if you kept a good name, and won praise and renown across the world: if His kindly glance doesn't fall on you, no one will ask after you. There's that word from pauri four: nadar, the gracious glance. Everything the world admires, long life, fame, followers, a good reputation, is stacked up as high as it can go, and then weighed against one glance, and the glance is heavier. Then the pauri gets sharper. Without that glance, it says, a person is like a worm among worms, and even wrongdoers point fingers at him. Strong words, but they're not an insult to anyone; they're a picture of how small fame really is, in the end. And then comes a turn toward mercy. Nanak, the One gives virtue to those who have none, and gives more virtue to the virtuous. And there's no one, the pauri says, who could give Him any virtue in return. So the whole thing flips. Fame is something the world hands out and takes back. Nadar is something only the Giver gives, freely, even to people who have nothing to show. It isn't that praise is wicked. Being thanked is lovely. It's that fame isn't it. It's not the thing that lasts, and it's not the thing that makes you matter.
screen: `FAMOUS IN ALL NINE REGIONS.` · `WITHOUT THE GLANCE, NO ONE ASKS.` · `A WORM AMONG WORMS.` · `VIRTUE GIVEN TO THE VIRTUELESS.` · then, large: `FAME IS NOT IT.`

segments.voice: Sit easily, and think of one place where you want to be praised right now. A post, a project, a family argument you want to be seen winning. Notice how it feels in your body: a small leaning forward, a waiting. Now, just for this bell, let the leaning go. Sit back. Imagine that no one ever finds out how good that thing was, and see what's left. Maybe there's still something good in it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru, who doesn't count likes. The bell holds the time.
Pauri seven. Live four ages and be famous everywhere; without the kindly glance of the One, no one asks after you.
Your line: fame is not it. Today, do one good thing and don't mention it to anyone, not even a hint. Day one hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the seventh pauri each morning; it is often quoted in talks on humility and on seva done without seeking praise.

match.prompt: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

myth: pauri seven says praise is wicked
it says fame isn't what lasts; without the glance, no one asks after you.
the One gives virtue even to those who have none
Nanak, He gives virtue to the virtueless, and more to the virtuous.
someone could give the One a virtue in return
there's no one who could give Him any virtue.

fork.setup: you've lived four ages and are famous in all nine regions. what does the pauri say happens without His kindly glance?
fork.reveal: je tis nadar na aavaee, ta vaat na puchhai ke: if the glance doesn't fall on you, no one asks after you.

original.note: Gurmukhi: to win praise and renown in the world (Japji, pauri 7).

trapdoor: what you thought: fame is bad.
what it means: fame isn't what lasts; only the kindly glance of the One does, and it's given freely.
what a scholar hears: the pauri pairs nirgun and gunvant, virtueless and virtuous: grace goes to both, and nothing can be given back.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 7

notes: Pauri 7 paraphrased after Macauliffe; not quoted.
'A worm among worms, and even wrongdoers point fingers' paraphrases 'keetaa andar keet kar dosee dos dhare'. Confirm.
Fork reveal quotes romanized Gurmukhi (not a translation): 'je tis nadar na aavaee ta vaat na puchhai ke'. Confirm romanization.
